title: Club ads, photographs in the black press, and the Million Dollar Room
summary: Discussion of why a black newspaper's ads used white figures, then Tex describes the Million Dollar Room, its pianists and 1950s drink prices.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Getting paid: wages, scale and the pay envelope

blocks.x: Well, I want you to look at this, the Tijuana Club ad. Is this kind of representative? I'm looking at these two people. Is this kind of representative?
In fact, these two people, in fact, it looks like there's two black, two white people here, in fact, in the ad.

Well, at that time, Ted, you've got to remember, even though it was a black newspaper, but when you lay the paper out, we did not have the cultured photographs at that time to put blacks, because the people who did these layouts, they did not have these black pictures to put into the picture, or into the advertised.
I would have thought a black newspaper, you would have put two blacks in the ad, and neither one of these ads.

What other words, it was cheaper to do it like this, because if you start putting color in it, then you've got another, because you've got to remember that most newspapers today even are printed in black and white, and when you start putting color in, you're dealing with more thousands and thousands of dollars. And then I'm thinking about the Million Dollar Room, which George Curry said, which was at the corner of Daniel and 6th Street in Uptown New Orleans. And the first time I walked into the club, you probably heard the name Laverne Smith, who was a cultured jazz pop piano player, who was a very tall, attractive woman, with a very golden smile. She could probably turn midnight into daylight just by smiling at you when she performed. She was a talented young lady. And also Walter Lewis was a jazz pianist who also appeared there from time to time. Then the Adams brother, Combo's, that was a family of all places on the West Bank of the River over in Algiers. And when you go back to the 50s, Mrs. Adams, the mother of the Adams family, she was a piano player. I can't think of her first name. Dolly Adams. She was a piano player also, so we're covering a lot of territory. But you've got to remember, in those days, highballs were 25 cents. Beer was 15 cents and 20 cents a bottle. And I can remember the old 4X beer was 5 cents a bottle. No, it was 10 cents a bottle. Westbrook, that's the first time I saw a 10-ounce beer, was 5 cents a bottle. Those were the glory days. Then you had Bernard's Hotel and Lounge, which was up in Proust Street. That was the area called Carrollton. You see, Carrollton, you may not believe this, but there's a story that a lot of people don't know about. But I'm going to try to relate it here as best I can. You probably heard talk of the city of Carrollton. In fact, it changed in 1852, and New Orleans somehow or another bought or either...
